item.title: Get Ready for Satoshi Mizukami’s Stunning Spirit Circle!
item.author: Nick Creamer
item.description: Spirit Circle getting an anime adaptation is a huge win
item.content:encoded: I have run through a fair number of “favorite manga” through the years, from the intimate, somewhat aspirational college drama of Shimoku Kio’s Genshiken as a teenager to the sublime paneling and dramatic formalism of Mitsuru Adachi’s Cross Game as a 20-something. However, it has in recent years seemed increasingly unlikely that I’ll be replacing my current favorite: the poignant, insightful, and wildly ambitious Spirit Circle , which I consider the best of Satoshi Mizukami’s altogether incredible catalog. As such, you can imagine my excitement when it was recently announced that Spirit Circle would be receiving an anime adaptation, particularly in the hands of such a talented director as Tatsuo Sato. And as I am nothing if not a hype man, I’m here to hopefully share at least a fragment of my enthusiasm with all of you. So, why should you all be excited for Spirit Circle ? Satoshi Mizukami Makes Incredible Things Mizukami’s mixture of absurdism and thoughtful humanism has long been understood by fans of his early manga like Lucifer and the Biscuit Hammer . In that story, an ostensibly farcical narrative about two kids who want to destroy the world ends up evolving into both a vivid battle manga and a stirring treatise on what it means to live, to share this life with others, and, through their presence, find meaning in our own. In more recent years, Mizukami has broken into the anime sphere through both regular adaptations and even an anime-original production, the magnificent Planet With . I rambled about Planet With’s manifold strengths at length back when it was first airing , but to keep things brief, the story serves as a multifaceted exploration of the nature of justice, challenging the thorny intersection of personal values and societal progress, all while delighting with charming characters like a bizarre man-shaped cat and a chipper maid-slash-princess. On both the micro level of its humor and fights and the macro level of its thematic ambitions, Planet With serves as a pocket-sized demonstration of Mizukami’s delightfully slanted perspective and thoughtful engagement with human nature, forgiving us all for the foibles that make us who we are. Tatsuo Sato Is a Terrific Director It was a tragic blow to learn of Tatsuo Sato’s passing this last spring after a career brimming with charming adventures and ambitious experiments. The man first rocketed into the spotlight with his very first full-length production, Martian Successor Nadesico . Though it was framed as a somewhat parodic take on the then-common genre of martial space adventures, Nadesico ultimately proved a gripping adventure in its own right, owing in large part to Sato’s distinctive eye for cinematic drama. In the wake of Nadesico , Sato lent his talents to an array of varied and often entrancing anime productions. His short film Cat Soup , based on a manga by Nekojiru, delivers a fantastical and ever-shifting journey into the afterlife, offering endless visual wonders while keenly striking at that childhood sensation of witnessing death before your time, like a nightmare you can only bear because you can’t fully comprehend it. His Shigofumi: Letters from the Departed offers a similarly poignant meditation on life after death, while even lighter productions like the charming, surprisingly grounded Bodacious Space Pirates demonstrate his theatrical sensibilities and easy way with humor. Given the course of his career, I couldn’t ask for a better director to realize Spirit Circle’s meditations on the meaning of life. Spirit Circle Is Superb Spirit Circle’s premise is ambitious from the start. A young boy is marked for death by his new classmate and must reexperience their many shared past lives in order to properly account for his crimes. This broad, roaming canvas affords Mizukami the space to genuinely measure the full meaning of a life, and in fact many lives, as our protagonist shifts from warrior to architect to scientist and beyond, exploring both the distant past and far future in search of vindication or justice. And yet time and again, he finds himself reaching the end of life with more questions than answers. Is the crime committed as a youth counterbalanced by the good enacted as an old man? Can a love unfulfilled still offer the sustenance of personal meaning, and is it even possible to truly understand one another? Why do we rise each day, knowing the certainty of tragedy and the inevitability of inflicting pain on others? Spirit Circle’s questions are impossible in scale, its answers finite and conditional. Yet chapter by chapter, past life by past life, a quiet refrain grows into a song of triumph as the small victories of a life spent in earnest congregate into a patchwork of human striving, a tapestry depicting all the beauty and love we share in vibrant, irresistible colors. Or something like that. As you can see, I get a little misty-eyed when I consider Spirit Circle’s personal dramas and thematic thrust; I suppose that’s how it goes when we discuss our very favorite stories. Regardless, I can attest that all that is great about Mizukami’s work is realized in glorious array throughout Spirit Circle . If you enjoy stories replete with off-kilter comedy and heart-on-sleeve emotions, you will surely find something to love in this upcoming production. I am eagerly awaiting its debut, and hope you’ll be there to join me!

item.title: Inu x Boku Secret Service Anime Celebrates 15th Anniversary with New Visual
item.author: Kara Dennison
item.description: Viewers in Japan can rewatch the entire 12-episode series
item.content:encoded: January 2027 marks the 15th anniversary of Inu x Boku Secret Service , the anime adaptation of Cocoa Fujiwara's manga of the same name. A new anniversary website opened to track upcoming activities for the occasion, including a rebroadcast in January and a new celebratory visual. Check out the new artwork from character designer and chief animation director Haruko Iizuka, featuring the cast in fancy attire: Inu x Boku Anime Anniversary Visual On January 8, 2027, TOKYO MX kicks off a rebroadcast of all 12 episodes. The anime adaptation of Cocoa Fujiwara's Inu x Boku Secret Service premiered in January 2012 and ran for 12 episodes and one OVA. Yen Press publishes the original manga under the title Inu x Boku SS , describing it thus: In search of independence and solitude, the sharp-tongued Ririchiyo Shirakiin moves to the Maison de Ayakashi, an apartment building full of wealthy tenants, which has its own Secret Service. Ririchiyo is eager to be alone, but upon her arrival, she is greeted by Soushi, an SS agent arranged for her by her parents. Ririchiyo tries to turn away, but Soushi's dogged devotion to his new mistress will not be deterred. The threats against the residents of the Maison de Ayakashi are not to be taken lightly, after all. And despite his puppylike demeanor, Soushi is not to be trifled with... Source: Official X (formerly Twitter) account

item.title: Peropero Sparkles Anime Premieres on January 10
item.author: Paul Chapman
item.description: Teaser trailer published for series based on mascot characters created by Yurie Sekiya
item.content:encoded: The upcoming Peropero Sparkles anime published a teaser trailer today. The series is scheduled to broadcast in Japan on the TV Tokyo network as part of the “Animori!” programming block beginning on January 10, 2027. Peropero Sparkles Teaser Trailer Peropero Sparkles is based on original work by Yurie Sekiya. Mao Miyashita directs the anime at animation studio Usagi Ou, with series composition by Yuji Umoto, character designs by Shiomi Yano and music by Shota Kowashi. The story of Peropero Sparkles follows Melo, Cune and Rue – a trio of mischievous creatures from the planet Peropero Sparkle – who visit Earth (after getting kicked out of their home world) in order to learn about the planet and its culture. Source: Peropero Sparkles at TV Tokyo ( 1 , 2 )
